arguments.text: Prop B will ensure that a San Francisco Public Bank is fiscally responsible, independent from political influence, and serves San Francisco’s priorities. A Public Bank puts the people of San Francisco over private profits to finance the things we need. The shareholders would be the people of San Francisco, so we benefit not only from our bank’s profits but also the San Francisco projects it supports. Prop B is a crucial step in creating a Public Bank. A Public Bank will provide affordable loans for: • Affordable housing development, • Affordable homeownership, • Small business development, • Environmental sustainability, and • Environmental justice. Prop B ensures that the Public Bank will be run by banking professionals, not politicians, and creates a public oversight body, so every San Franciscan has the opportunity to monitor and provide input. A public bank is about making sure San Franciscans’ money benefits San Franciscans. Passing Prop B now allows us to take advantage of the time-limited state law that enables local cities to create public banks. A public bank creates a powerful new tool to address some of our city’s most urgent priorities. Public banking is a proven development model. Globally 25% of banking assets are held in public banks, and Germany holds 40% of its banking assets in public banks. Prop B establishes the purpose and structure of a public bank. Prop B is not a tax, and will not raise taxes for San Franciscans.

arguments.text: San Francisco’s financial support for housing, infrastructure and small business is limited for good reason. Proposition B empowers the far left to dismantle and politicize those limits. A “public bank” is a politically directed lending machine that puts billions of taxpayer dollars at risk. The Controller estimates $310-$460 million just to capitalize and operate it. Once the Bank takes deposits, the City can park rainy-day funds and investment-pool reserves inside it, multiplying the risk by lending and leverage. The Bank can issue securities bought by the City itself. High-risk loans inevitably go bad; the losses land on taxpayers. Public banking has a litany of failure. The Los Angeles Community Development Bank collapsed under a mountain of bad loans. Any bank whose mission is climate-justice, racial preferences and loans refused by private lenders is fundamentally unsound. California law requires FDIC insurance; no public bank has successfully obtained it while pursuing this radical agenda. Nothing in Proposition B meaningfully checks the Bank’s political priorities. Pressure will build for reparations-style lending and loans to non-citizens, unleashing a smear of red ink across the general fund. This is the same socialist model in Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib’s Public Banking Act, co-sponsored by Ilhan Omar and the Squad. Don’t be a piker. Vote No on Proposition B.

arguments.text: Vote No on Proposition B. Proposition B asks San Francisco voters to create a City Hall-controlled public bank and municipal finance corporation — without any dedicated funding, without proven demand, and at a time when the City already faces massive budget shortfalls. Supporters claim this will unlock affordable housing and small business lending. In reality, it creates a new politically appointed entity with the power to take significant financial risks using public resources. The City’s own working group previously estimated hundreds of millions of dollars would be needed to capitalize such an institution. Proposition B provides none of that capital. It simply builds the structure and leaves taxpayers holding the bag later. San Francisco already has tools to support housing and small businesses through existing programs, nonprofit lenders, and credit unions. Creating a new City-controlled bank adds bureaucracy, political risk, and potential conflicts of interest without solving the underlying problems of high costs and slow permitting. We cannot afford another ambitious, underfunded experiment. Vote No on Proposition B.

arguments.text: Proposition B is a simple measure. It establishes a San Francisco Public Bank, which could help fund housing, green energy, and small businesses, and sets rules to prevent the bank or its funds from being misused. As the opponents point out, Prop B is NOT a tax and will not raise taxes on residents or businesses. Opponents claim that the bank would be rife with political instability and risky lending, but that is untrue. Instead, it would be the most regulated bank in America, subject to all typical banking regulations of private banks, in addition to California regulations and the oversight systems of Prop B. Prop B empowers San Francisco to pursue funding for our bank from state, federal, and philanthropic sources. Opportunities like the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund in Biden’s Climate bill present billions of dollars San Francisco could access. These are opportunities we have missed out on because we do not have a MFC or Public Bank. We must pass Prop B to be ready for these generational opportunities. A Public Bank would support our existing nonprofit, city, and credit union ecosystem, making the most efficient use of taxpayer money. We can’t afford to miss this opportunity to build an economic engine to stabilize San Francisco and make sure money is going where it’s needed, for housing, green energy, and supporting our small businesses.

arguments.heading: Prop B is the thoughtful, safe, and fiscally responsible way to create a public bank
arguments.text: Public banks solve many problems and provide tremendous value for communities across the world. 25% of the world’s banking assets are held in public banks because they work well at reinvesting public funds to support development. But in order to deliver these massive benefits they must remain politically independent and committed to fiscal responsibility. Prop B ensures that our public bank is established with robust governance and best practices. Prop B requires that our Public Bank • Has an independent board of directors who make all key decisions. • Has an oversight committee with appointments spread across elected offices. • Has multiple safeguards to ensure no single politician can exercise influence on lending decisions. • Be run by professional bankers working for the people of San Francisco, not politicians. • Partner with experts in local finance: local credit unions, Community Development Financial Institutions (CDFIs), and community banks. Prop B creates a Public Bank that all San Franciscans can trust.

arguments.heading: Prop B is the culmination of years of rigorous work:
arguments.text: • In 2017 the San Francisco Public Bank Coalition was founded. • In 2019, the California State Assembly successfully passed AB 857, the California Public Banking Act, creating a formal pathway for local jurisdictions to charter their own public banks to save money, strengthen our local economies, support community economic development, and address our critical infrastructure and housing needs. • In 2021, the Board of Supervisors passed an ordinance establishing the San Francisco Reinvestment Working Group to oversee the formation of a business and governance plan, consisting of the Controller, Treasurer, and technical experts in financial institutions, affordable housing financing, small business lending, environmental justice, and renewable energy. • The Reinvestment Working Group hired an experienced banking consultant who has started over 100 banks and worked with them to prepare a Final Governance Plan, Business Plan, and Viability Study for a San Francisco Municipal Financial Corporation and a San Francisco Public Bank, which were accepted by the Board of Supervisors in 2023. The years of rigorous work by city leaders across the political spectrum and movement work by advocates have produced this thoroughly vetted plan for a successful Public Bank that forms the basis of this Charter Amendment.

proposal.value: Proposition B would amend the City Charter to authorize the City to establish a municipal finance corporation if the City has sufficient funding and resources. After three years of operation, the municipal finance corporation may become a public bank. The MFC would make loans but would not take deposits. If the MFC becomes a public bank, the public bank would make loans and also take deposits. The MFC and public bank would provide services to support: • affordable housing development, • affordable homeownership, • small business development, • environmental sustainability, and • environmental justice. These services would be available to individual City residents and to projects and businesses located in the City. Under Proposition B, the MFC and public bank would each be governed by a board of directors. Each board would be appointed and overseen by its own oversight commission. The members of each oversight commission would be appointed by the Board of Supervisors, Mayor, Treasurer-Tax Collector, Controller, and City Attorney.

way_it_is_now.value: A municipal finance corporation (MFC) is a government-owned non-profit corporation that makes loans but does not take deposits. A public bank is a government-owned non-profit corporation that both makes loans and takes deposits. There is no local law authorizing the City to create a municipal finance corporation or a public bank.

effects.text: Capitalization and funding amounts depend on future decisions by the MFC Board of Directors and by the Mayor and Board of Supervisors; costs may be higher or lower than the 2023 RWG estimates.

citations.quote: The capitalization and funding costs are choices dependent on future decisions by the MFC Board of Directors and future policy and budget decisions by the Mayor and the Board of Supervisors. The costs associated with establishing an MFC may be significantly higher or lower than the 2023 RWG estimates.
citations.locator: p. 71, Controller's Statement on "B", left column, paragraph beginning "In 2022"

effects.text: If the City establishes an MFC and then a Public Bank: about $310 million to $460 million over eight years (2023 RWG estimates); could be higher or lower with interest rates and economic conditions.

citations.quote: However, if the City moves forward with establishing a MFC and subsequently a Public Bank, as authorized by the proposed Charter amendment, the costs would be significant, ranging from approximately $310 million to $460 million over an eight-year period, according to 2023 Reinvestment Working Group (RWG) estimates, which could be significantly higher or lower depending on interest rates and changing economic conditions.
citations.locator: p. 70, Controller's Statement on "B", paragraph 1

effects.text: MFC capitalization and funding (2023 RWG): about $26 million in year one rising to $30 million a year by year three, $90 million over three years; levels explored ranged from $45 million to $242 million.

citations.quote: According to a 2023 report of the RWG, costs to capitalize and fund the MFC could cost approximately $26 million in the first year and increase to $30 million annually by the third year for a total of $90 million for the first three years of the MFC. The RWG explored a variety of capitalization and funding levels including cumulative totals of $45 million to $242 million over the first three years. Capitalization and funding costs could be financed by City grants and forgivable loans which are unlikely to be repaid.
citations.locator: p. 71, Controller's Statement on "B", left column, paragraph beginning "In 2022"

effects.text: If an MFC is set up: about $4 million a year for about one year or longer (staff, legal and professional services, technology, administration), excluding capitalization.

citations.quote: The funding required to set up an MFC could cost approximately $4 million annually for approximately one year or longer, depending on when the MFC is set up, excluding capitalization costs. These costs include the cost to hire staff, staff salaries, legal services, supporting professional services, technology procurement and administrative operations.
citations.locator: p. 71, Controller's Statement on "B", left column, paragraph on MFC setup funding

effects.text: Would not directly affect the cost of government, because the amendment does not require the City to create an MFC or Public Bank.

citations.quote: Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would not directly impact the cost of government as the Charter amendment does not require the City to create a Municipal Finance Corporation (MFC) that could transition into a Public Bank.
citations.locator: p. 70, Controller's Statement on "B", paragraph 1

effects.text: MFC or Bank Oversight Commission: $550,000 to $600,000 a year for staff salaries, commissioner stipends and operating costs.

citations.quote: Finally, the MFC and Public Bank would require an MFC Oversight Commission or Bank Oversight Commission which could cost between $550,000 to $600,000 annually for staff salaries, commissioner stipends, and operating costs.
citations.locator: p. 71, Controller's Statement on "B", left column, paragraph beginning "Finally"

effects.text: If the MFC becomes a Public Bank: about $80 million in year 4, then about $30 million to $40 million a year, about $220 million over years 4 to 8; Bank income may reduce the City funding needed.

citations.quote: In the event the MFC becomes financially sustainable and receives regulatory approval to operate as a depository bank, it may become a Public Bank. The cost to operate a Public Bank would be approximately $80 million in year 4, decreasing to approximately $30 to $40 million annually for a total of approximately $220 million over years four through eight. These costs include capital funds and operating costs, including staff salaries, office leases, technology, and administrative costs. The Public Bank may use its income to fund its operating costs if available, requiring less funding appropriated by the City.
citations.locator: p. 71, Controller's Statement on "B", left column, paragraph beginning "In the event the MFC becomes financially sustainable and receives"

effects.text: Possible unforeseen costs to the City if the Public Bank is not financially sustainable; not estimated. The statement notes a high degree of uncertainty in the cost of an MFC or Public Bank.

citations.quote: There is a high degree of uncertainty in the cost to government of establishing an MFC or Public Bank. There may be significant unforeseen costs to the City in the event the Public Bank is not financially sustainable.

summary.summary: Should the proposed Charter amendment be approved by the voters, in my opinion, it would not directly impact the cost of government as the Charter amendment does not require the City to create a Municipal Finance Corporation (MFC) that could transition into a Public Bank. However, if the City moves forward with establishing a MFC and subsequently a Public Bank, as authorized by the proposed Charter amendment, the costs would be significant, ranging from approximately $310 million to $460 million over an eight-year period, according to 2023 Reinvestment Working Group (RWG) estimates, which could be significantly higher or lower depending on interest rates and changing economic conditions.
